title: Proxy handshake amplification and stream synchrony matrix
content:
Purpose:
Investigate how client flush cadence, proxy hop count, and TLS/HTTP multiplexing interact to amplify tail latency for streaming inference responses. This is a working note — rough sketches, microbench outputs and mitigation proposals. Goal is to surface concrete heuristics we can add to edge proxy and SDK defaults to avoid pathological latency amplification in real workloads.

Context / why this surfaced:
- Multiple production incidents in Feb where long-tail streaming requests spiked P99 by 2-3x after a traffic shift (model rollout + increased short-prompt volume).
- Hypothesis from initial triage: combination of very frequent small client flushes (~1-2 tokens per flush), an additional egress proxy hop (customer edge + our regional proxy), and TLS record coalescing behavior caused synchronized bursts and head-of-line amplification.

Quick summary of findings:
1) Small flush size + N proxy hops -> near-linear amplification of per-chunk overhead. For our test rig with 3 proxy hops, median per-chunk latency increased ~3x relative to single hop.
2) TLS record/handshake costs were not dominant for long-lived connections, but TLS record emission timing (Nagle-like coalescing) on different hops caused micro-batching misalignment and added 5-30ms per chunk in the worst cases.
3) HTTP/2 stream prioritization plus proxy ingress queueing caused occasional reordering of chunk delivery which increased tail latency; gRPC over HTTP/2 showed similar effects but callbacks at client SDK layer hid some of it.
4) Simple server-side aggregation (buffer up to X bytes or Y ms) reduced P99 significantly with minimal P50 regression for typical prompt sizes.

Testbed and methodology:
- Cluster: 2 client machines (golang SDK harness), 3 proxy layers (envoy-based edge -> internal proxy -> regional proxy), single inference backend (pinned model instance). All proxies configured with realistic timeouts and default TCP/TLS settings.
- Network: within same AZ, <1ms base RTT; introduced synthetic RTT to emulate cross-region of +30ms in some runs.
- Workloads: synthetic token streams of varying token-flush patterns:
  - micro: client flushes 1 token every 8ms
  - sparse: 1 token every 25ms
  - bursty: 8 tokens every 40ms
  - aligned: 4 tokens every 16ms (aligned to proxy flush windows)
- Measurements: per-chunk latency at client, per-hop egress/inbound timestamps (where possible), socket write timestamps, TLS record emit timestamps from tcpdump + OpenSSL trace when feasible.
- Runs: 10k requests per pattern, run across 3 proxy hop configs (0,1,3).

Representative numbers (median / P95 / P99 in ms) - micro pattern:
- 0 hops: P50 18, P95 32, P99 48
- 1 hop: P50 22, P95 56, P99 92
- 3 hops: P50 36, P95 124, P99 218
Notes: numbers include both application and networking serialization. Amplification higher in P99 than in median.

Observation threads (raw notes):
- Socket-level batching: Linux TCP stack + application writes lead to small bursts being sent as multiple TLS records. Proxy A aggregated differently than Proxy B leading to misalignment: proxy A coalesced quickly (lower threshold), proxy B held for Nagle-like window and then flushed, creating a 10-30ms gap.
- TLS records sizing: when client sends 1-2 byte JSON chunks (very small), they end up as separate TLS records and are unpacked at each hop — each hop processing adds scheduling jitter.
- HTTP/2 frame multiplexing: at the internal proxy we saw frames for unrelated streams interleave; priority algorithm increased latency for some streaming streams (lower priority).
- Backpressure signals: gRPC-level flow control windows sometimes caused upstream to stall briefly which then manifested as microbursts downstream; combined with small client flushes this created synchronized pressure.

Hypothesis exploration experiments:
- Experiment A: increase client SDK write coalescing to group up to 16 bytes or wait 6ms before flush. Result: P99 improved by ~40% on 3-hop tests.
- Experiment B: proxy ingress soft-threshold: buffer up to 128 bytes or 8ms then flush. Result: P99 improved with negligible P50 change for sparse and bursty patterns; micro pattern P50 rose by ~4ms but P99 fell ~55%.
- Experiment C: disable HTTP/2 stream reprioritization at internal proxy. Result: mixed; some streams improved but others regressed because reprioritization prevented head-of-line blocking in other cases.
- Experiment D: simulate additional 30ms per-hop RTT. Result: amplification multiplies; mitigation from coalescing still effective but larger ms windows needed for coalescing (15-25ms) to offset added RTT cost which starts to harm latency for single-hop short RTT cases.

Mitigation proposals (prioritized):
1) SDK defaults: enable small, inexpensive client-side coalescing by default. Configurable parameters: max_coalesce_bytes=32, max_coalesce_ms=8. Rationale: most apps benefit and it prevents pathological flush-of-one-token.
2) Edge proxy heuristic: implement adaptive flush threshold that tracks recent per-stream interarrival and autocorrelates across hops. If upstream is sending sub-16B chunks at <10ms spacing, buffer up to 12ms or 128 bytes. Expose as feature flag.
3) Telemetry: emit per-request "chunking-profile" metadata (avg chunk size, flush rate, hop-count) to backend traces so we can detect client patterns that harm latency and surface in Console.
4) Backpressure tuning: make gRPC flow-control window growth slightly more aggressive for streaming inference streams (experimental flag) so upstream producers avoid short stalls.
5) Proxy hop reduction guidance: for customers with high short-message workloads recommend a single-edge-proxy design or in-path bypass where the client can reach regional proxy directly.

Potential downsides and risks:
- Coalescing adds small additional latency for very low-latency single-hop scenarios; need to default conservatively and allow per-route overrides.
- Buffering in proxies increases memory pressure and could interact poorly with very high concurrency unless soft-limits are enforced.
- Changing flow-control aggressiveness could expose server to higher instantaneous write bursts; we need to monitor for increased CPU/IO.

Open questions / follow-ups:
- How do real customer SDK patterns look? We need to sample chunking-profile telemetry (opt-in) from staging customers to verify distribution and pick defaults.
- Should we expose a per-route policy in Console that allows customers to pick "low-latency short-chunks" vs "throughput-optimized" presets?
- Deeper kernel/TCP tuning: would coalescing interplay with TCP_CORK or MSG_MORE deliver better results on our proxies? Quick experiments planned.
- Can we detect pathological client libraries (e.g., they flush per-char) and auto-suggest or auto-inject a client-side coalescing shim for hosted flows?

Action items (owners & timelines):
- Priya: prototype SDK coalescing in golang/python SDKs and run canary on internal dev org (2 weeks).
- Marco: implement adaptive proxy buffer heuristic in internal proxy (feature-flagged) and run a performance sweep (3 weeks).
- Sofia & Ethan: instrumentation changes to emit chunking-profile and a Console dashboard to visualize per-route patterns (4 weeks).
- SRE: add stress tests for memory behavior when buffering enabled (2 weeks).

Appendix: sample trace excerpt (simplified)
- client write timestamps: 0ms, 8ms, 16ms, 24ms... (1 token writes)
- proxy A egress: 0ms, 9ms, 17ms, 26ms (proxy added 1-2ms jitter)
- proxy B egress: 0ms, 28ms, 56ms... (proxy B coalesced and flushed in larger batches)
- client observed per-chunk delivery at 6ms, 32ms, 58ms -> shows amplification and grouping mismatch

Notes to self (quick):
- Keep this doc lightweight — convert to Confluence once we have prototype numbers.
- Cross-reference with spike incidents: incident-20250218-stream-tail-latency.

If we move forward: propose a small opt-in pilot: enable SDK coalescing + internal adaptive buffer on a subset of backend pools to measure production impact over 2 weeks before default rollback/enable.
